topic: The Collision-Pi Connection: Why Bouncing Blocks Compute Pi
target_audience: High school physics students and undergraduate mathematics enthusiasts

sections.title: The Strange Setup: A Counting Mystery
lecture_lines: Imagine a frictionless floor with a wall on the left.
A small block and a massive block sit nearby.
The large block slides in, starting a chain of collisions.
animations: Create a horizontal line (#FFFFFF) for the floor and a wall [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/wall.svg] at the left edge.

Add a small green block [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/block.svg] (mass m, #00FF00) and a large blue block [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/block.svg] (mass M, #0000FF) to the right of the wall.

The large blue block [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/block.svg] moves left, striking the small green block [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/block.svg]; use a flash effect (#FFFFFF) for every collision.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Laws of the Game
lecture_lines: Momentum is conserved as the blocks push each other.
Kinetic energy is also preserved in these elastic bounces.
These two laws define the outcome of every collision.
animations: Display the Conservation of Momentum equation: 'm v_1 + M v_2 = \text{const}' in yellow (#FFFF00) accompanied by the blocks icon [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/blocks.svg].
Display the Conservation of Energy equation: '1/2 m v_1^2 + 1/2 M v_2^2 = E' in cyan (#00FFFF).
Highlight both equations with a white rectangle (#FFFFFF) to indicate they are the governing laws.

sections.title: The Pattern Emerges: Scaling the Mass
lecture_lines: With equal masses, we count exactly three collisions.
At a hundred-to-one ratio, thirty-one collisions occur.
Increasing the mass further reveals a startling pattern.
The count perfectly matches the digits of Pi.
This mechanical system actually computes the constant Pi.
animations: Show a simulation with M=1 and m=1; the collision count '3' appears in white (#FFFFFF) above the blocks.
Show M=100 and m=1; the collision count increments to '31' in white (#FFFFFF).
Show M=10,000 and m=1; the collision count increments to '314' in white (#FFFFFF).
Flash the digits '314' in pink (#FF00FF) to emphasize the connection to Pi.
Display the symbol 'pi' (#FF00FF) as the mass ratio increases further to 1,000,000.

sections.title: The Geometry of Velocity: Mapping to a Circle
lecture_lines: We map these velocities onto a geometric plane.
Rescaling the axes transforms our equations into a circle.
Energy conservation keeps the system on this circle's edge.
Each block-to-block collision is a jump along the circle.
Wall collisions reflect the point across the vertical axis.
animations: Draw coordinate axes labeled v1 and v2 in grey (#888888).
Update axis labels to x = sqrt(m)v1 and y = sqrt(M)v2 using white text (#FFFFFF).
Draw a cyan circle (#00FFFF) centered at the origin, representing the conservation of energy.
A point representing the system's state jumps to a new position on the circle for each collision between blocks [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/block.svg].
The point reflects across the y-axis for each collision between the small block [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/block.svg] and the wall.

sections.title: The Angle of Pi: Why the Counting Works
lecture_lines: Every hit moves the point by a fixed arc angle.
This angle depends on the ratio of the masses.
The point travels along the perimeter of the circle.
We count how many steps fit into half the circle.
The final count reveals the digits of Pi.
animations: Highlight a single arc segment on the circle and label its angle as 'theta' (#FFFF00).
Show the relationship theta = arctan(sqrt(m/M)) in yellow text (#FFFF00).
Animate the circle filling up with arcs of size theta, starting from the positive x-axis.
Show that the total number of steps is the number of times theta fits into the semi-circle (pi radians).
Display the final equation: 'Number of collisions = floor(pi / theta)' in white (#FFFFFF).

sections.title: Conclusion: Physics as a Computer
lecture_lines: This system acts as a mechanical computer for Pi.
It reveals a deep link between dynamics and geometry.
Mathematical beauty emerges from the simplest physical laws.
animations: Animate a fast-forward of the block simulation [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/computer.svg] with a massive mass ratio, with the collision counter spinning rapidly.
The counter stops at '3,141,592', which is highlighted in green (#00FF00).
Fade out the blocks and equations, leaving only the large symbol 'pi' (#FFFFFF) center-stage.
